bib.title: Bandit Algorithms, Chapter 38: Markov Decision Processes

question: How can a learner compete with the optimal average-reward policy in an unknown finite MDP, and what regret is achievable and necessary?
contributions: Defines finite MDPs, diameter and the average-reward (gain) optimality criterion with the Bellman optimality equation.
Gives LP-based computation of optimal policies.
Presents UCRL2 with regret bound O(D S sqrt(A n log n)) and a matching-in-n lower bound Omega(sqrt(DSAn)).

limits: Upper and lower bounds differ by a factor of at least sqrt(DS); the authors call the gap considerable.
Assumes strongly connected MDP (finite diameter); UCRL2 is brittle with unreachable states (Note 13).
Rewards assumed known and deterministic in the main text; unknown rewards left to Ex 38.23.
Bounds are vacuous for large state spaces without extra structure (Note 1).
Ellipsoid-based polynomial time is impractical; value/policy iteration works better in practice (Note 12).
Agrawal and Jia 2017 proof said to be not quite correct; Bartlett and Tewari 2009 Theorem 4 proof said to be incorrect (Ex 38.13).
Only the average-reward setting is treated in depth; discounting appears in exercises and notes.
practices: Restrict to strongly connected MDPs, otherwise learning against an informed agent is hopeless (Sec 38.1).
Use phases that end when a state-action count doubles rather than re-planning every round, to avoid dithering and linear regret (Sec 38.5, Ex 38.19).
Choose the state so it is observable and satisfies the Markov property; enlarging the state slows learning (Note 2).
Prefer value or policy iteration over the ellipsoid method in practice (Note 12).
Subtract max v each step in value iteration to keep numbers bounded (Note 12).

terms.definition: An MDP is defined by a tuple M = (S, A, P, r, µ). The first two items S and A are sets called the state space and action space
memoryless policies, which choose actions based on only the current state, possibly in a randomised manner
A trap is a subset of the state space from which there is no escape.
for any pair of states s, s′ ∈S, there exists a policy such that when starting from s there is a positive probability of reaching s′ some time in the future while following the policy
D(M) = max over s != s' of min over deterministic memoryless pi of E_pi[min{t>=1: S_t = s} | S_1 = s'] - 1 (Definition 38.1)
The gain of a policy π is the long-term average reward expected from using that policy when starting in state s
v_pi = lim (1/n) sum_k v_pi^(k) = ((I - P_pi + P*_pi)^-1 - P*_pi) r_pi, the Cesaro sum of (P_pi^t (r_pi - rho_pi))
a deterministic memoryless policy πv given by πv(s) = argmaxa∈A ra(s) + ⟨Pa(s), v⟩
(Tv)(s) = max_a r_a(s) + <P_a(s), v>; Bellman optimality equation is rho 1 + v = Tv
state space S and state-dependent action space {(a, P): a in A, P in C_tau_k(s,a)}; the agent picks both the action and a plausible transition vector
A state s ∈S is absorbing if Pa(s, s) = 1 for all a ∈A. An MDP is episodic if there exists an absorbing state that is reached almost surely by any policy.
a generalisation where the learner does not observe the underlying state; instead receives an observation that is a function of the state
Cesaro sum is lim (1/n)(s_1+...+s_n) of partial sums; Abel sum is lim_{gamma->1} of the gamma-discounted average; the two agree when the Cesaro sum exists (vanishing discount approach)
A memoryless policy π∗is bias optimal if it is gain optimal and vπ∗≥vπ for all memoryless policies π
